articles.title: ‘Why would he do this to us?’: Trump's foreign beef push is hurting his base, Republicans warn
articles.summary: Republican lawmakers warn President Donald Trump that his foreign beef import order is hurting loyal cattle ranchers ahead of the midterm elections.
articles.body: Republicans are warning President Donald Trump that his decision to flood supermarkets with foreign ground beef is hurting a key group in his base as the midterm elections near their climax. Voters in beef-industry-heavy states, like South Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas, supported Trump in his bid for a second term. Now, lawmakers from those states say his decision to lift tariffs on hundreds of thousands of tons of foreign beef is putting the very people who elected him in a bind. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., who is running for re-election, said his voters in South Dakota "love the president," and view him like a member of the family, but the beef import order feels like the administration "pulled the rug right out from underneath" them. TRUMP WANTS CHEAPER BEEF. REPUBLICANS IN KEY RACES WARN HIS PLAN GOES TOO FAR "They're hurt. I mean, they feel like they've been let down," Rounds said. "Like, how could, you know, our friend, this guy that's as close to us as they've ever been to a president, how could he do this to them? I mean, that's the way they feel," he continued. "And that's the expression they're giving me is, ‘Why would he do this to us? Doesn't he understand ag?’" Republicans are searching for an economic message to bring to voters as grocery bills, gas prices and other day-to-day necessities grow more expensive. Some argue that kneecapping ranchers and farmers, some of Trump’s most loyal supporters, in the name of affordability runs counter to that. "I think people want an explanation," a House Republican granted anonymity to speak freely told Fox News Digital. "We want to be able to go to the ranchers, who are big Trump supporters, right, to be able to go to them and say, this administration is fighting for you." THE UNEXPECTED FORCE KEEPING BEEF PRICES HIGH AND WHY THE PRESSURE COULD LAST FOR YEARS Trump signed the order last week with the intent of flooding the market with 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef, lowering costs for consumers thanks to a commitment that the product would be sold at 25% below current market prices over a 90-day span. He also contended that it would allow ranchers to regrow the nation’s herds, which, thanks to a combination of drought and the invasive New World screwworm, has dwindled to historic lows not seen since the 1950s, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). "I’m sympathetic to what he’s trying to get done," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Keloland. "He’s trying to lower beef prices, which I think we’re all supportive of. I just don’t think this is the way to do it. And so, we have a lot of beef producers here in South Dakota; they produce the highest-quality beef in the world, and we’re trying to build our herds back up." As the blowback mounts, the administration has acknowledged that ranchers are bearing the brunt of the blow. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer huddled privately with House Republicans on Wednesday afternoon, when several lawmakers pressed him on the subject of Trump’s beef imports. NEBRASKA RANCHERS STRUGGLE TO RECOVER FROM HISTORIC WILDFIRES AS DROUGHT WORSENS CRISIS Sources inside the room told Fox News Digital that Greer acknowledged ranchers were frustrated but maintained the import strategy was temporary. He argued it was the administration’s way of easing high prices on the market in the short term, the sources said. But multiple House GOP lawmakers still said they were concerned as they exited the meeting. "This is not just a one-year issue on the affordability of beef. We’ve got to make sure that we’ve got a Made-in-America-first beef program. That means standing with our cattlemen on that," Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, told Fox News Digital. "We’ve said the same thing to [Greer] in there." Nunn, who is a top target for Democrats in November, said he planned to raise the issue again during dinner with Trump at the White House on Wednesday evening. Rep. Troy Downing, R-Mont., pointed out that it was a relatively small amount of beef for just a 90-day period but said he was worried about the timing as it overlaps with the time of year farmers bring their cattle to market. "If a rancher is expecting to get a price at market that suddenly drops out from underneath them, they’re faced with two things — they don’t have a stable market, so do I invest in heifers for next year? Or do I have to sell more calves to make up for that deficit for my operating costs? Which, neither one is helping rebuild the herd," Downing told Fox News Digital. House Main Street Caucus Chairman Mike Flood, R-Neb., said he was opposed to a "tariff regime that undercuts American ranchers," but said Trump’s policies were helping in the "big picture." Compounding people’s anxiety in the meeting was Trump’s trade war with Canada, which that House Republican said made northern-border-state GOP lawmakers "nervous." Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital there would likely be "quite a few" follow-up meetings. "It was absolutely outstanding, we had a tremendous amount of participation and people that were really excited to ask good questions," he said of the meeting in general. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said at an event in Iowa on Tuesday that the administration understood that "ranchers felt like that was a gut punch." The White House argued that Trump "has done more for American agriculture than anyone" with trade deals, foreign market access expansion, lowering input costs, bolstering the farm safety net, doubling the death tax exemption, ending taxes on rural property loan interest, and creating rural opportunity zones." "At the same time, he is delivering on his promise to consumers by reducing beef prices while allowing our American beef herd to grow," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told Fox News Digital. "The President will continue taking actions to support our great farmers while driving economic prosperity for all Americans." Republican critics of the move are urging the administration to look at other methods to expand the nation’s cattle herds. Several Republicans, led by Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., wrote to Rollins and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to lift Biden-era rules and ease federal guardrails to allow for more access to grazing land for cattle. "The Federal government must remain laser-focused on partnering with the industry and state efforts for ranchers, expand grazing on public and private lands, and improve protein processing capacity," they wrote in a letter to the top Trump officials on Tuesday.

articles.title: Vance's Antichrist comments are a 'common belief', his friend tells BBC
articles.summary: The US vice-president recently mused with a Christian podcast host on whether the end of the world was nigh.
articles.body:
Recent remarks by US Vice-President JD Vance about the Antichrist and "the end times" are a "very, very common belief", one of his friends says.

Vance recently mused on his religious views while responding to a question on a Christian podcast. He said he would "not [be] shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us" and speculated on whether the end of the world was nigh.

His friend Rod Dreher, a conservative writer, rejected any suggestion that the comments would harm the vice-president. He told the BBC's Today programme: "Most Americans who are inclined to vote Republican already believe this stuff."

In his podcast comments, Vance also clarified that such thoughts did not preoccupy him.

In Christianity, the "end times" phrase refers to theories about what will happen at the end of the world. Many churches believe God has a divine plan for the end of everything.

Meanwhile, the Antichrist is seen as the enemy of God who appears during the final phase of the world's existence and takes it over.

Vance, who became a Catholic as an adult, reflected on these topics during a recent podcast discussion with Bryce Crawford, a US Christian podcaster.

"Do I think that we're in the end times? I don't know," he said in response to a Crawford question on the subject. "And I think that it's probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it, because there are, like, things you gotta do.

"I gotta be good to my wife. I gotta be good to my kids. I have to be as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America."

The vice-president continued by saying: "I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us."

But Vance reiterated that he was preoccupied with being vice-president, explaining: "What I'm trying to focus on is doing as much of God's work as possible right now."

Reacting to Vance's comments about the Antichrist, Dreher said: "This might sound bonkers to someone who is outside the Christian religion, but it is a very, very common belief within Christianity."

He said his friend was simply reflecting that the world appeared to be going "crazy" through the rapid development of AI and ongoing conflicts.

Dreher, who was present when Vance was received into the Catholic Church, said Ronald Reagan had made similar comments when he was the US president, and that this was seen as "perfectly normal" by his voters.

Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019, then in his mid-30s, and has described how the Church resonated with his family and social values and his conservative politics.

Since becoming vice-president, he has occasionally tangled with Pope Leo and his papal predecessor Francis, on issues including the Trump administration's immigration policy.

Vance is due to appear behind the lectern on Thursday afternoon to deliver the first White House press briefing since the departure of Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

articles.title: Days are about to get way shorter in September: How much daylight we’re losing
articles.summary: The days will still have 24 hours, of course, but the amount of daylight you see is declining.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – The calendars have officially flipped to September, which means fall is basically upon us , bringing the prospect of cooler temperatures, changing leaves, and, unfortunately, shorter days.

At least, the days will start feeling shorter. They still have 24 hours in them, as they always do. But we’re about to see less and less daylight as the month goes on.

Through September’s end, some parts of the country will lose more than an hour of daylight compared to where they stand now. In many cases, sunsets will start happening before 7 p.m. , a trend that won’t change for months.

It’s all because of Earth’s tilt and orbit. During this time of year, the sun hits the northern hemisphere more indirectly, reducing how much daylight we get.

It’s those living in the northern portions of the U.S. that stand to lose the most daylight through September. Bismarck, North Dakota, for example, will have lost about 95 minutes of daylight by the time October begins. Further west in Portland, Oregon, Sept. 30 will be about one and a half hours shorter than Sept. 1.

The interactive table below shows how much daylight 60 U.S. cities will lose this month:

The best off is Honolulu, Hawaii, where there is only about a 34-minute difference in the amount of daylight the city sees between the start and end of September. Its lack of lost sunlight was a contributing factor in the state’s decision to observe standard time year-round .

Between now and the day that every other clock in the U.S. falls back to standard time, the aforementioned cities will have lost about twice the daylight they lose in September alone. Through October, Bismarck’s daylight will decline by about 96 minutes – combined with September, that’s a loss of more than three hours of daylight by Nov. 1.

Nov. 1 will, in a way, be the longest day of the year. At 2 a.m., our clocks are set to “fall back” to 1 a.m., essentially giving us an extra hour in the day.

That long day may be nonexistent, though, should the Senate pass the Sunshine Protection Act upon returning from recess. The bill, which has received President Trump’s support since passing through the House, would make daylight saving time permanent . While you would notice an impact , the move would not add to the amount of daylight hours we experience during winter.

Unless the Senate takes up and passes the Sunshine Protection Act soon, you can expect your clocks to fall back an hour on Nov. 1.

articles.title: Black women are poised for historic congressional gains in November
articles.summary: With nearly all primaries concluded, 77 Black women have secured spots on midterm ballots.
articles.body:
Black women candidates could make historic gains in the November midterm elections. That’s good news for all Americans, because it’s a sign our country is overcoming centuries of racism and sexism to take advantage of everyone’s talents.

Data shared with me by Rutgers’ Center for American Women in Politics and Higher Heights shows that with nearly all primaries concluded, 77 Black women have secured spots on midterm ballots as candidates for the U.S. House and Senate, governorships and other statewide offices. Seventy-one are Democrats.

The Black women who get elected will make America even greater than it already is because our nation’s diversity enables all types of people to combine their differing knowledge, experiences and perspectives to work together to build a better future for us all. Black women have a lot to contribute when given the chance.

A total of 44 Black women — 41 of them Democrats — have been nominated to run for the U.S. House from 20 states and the Virgin Islands. The current House session began with 27 Black women serving as representatives and two others serving as nonvoting delegates from Washington, D.C., and the Virgin Islands. All 29 are Democrats.

Four Black women Democrats have been nominated to run for the U.S. Senate in the midterms from Florida, Illinois, Oklahoma and Tennessee. Two Black women Democrats are now serving as senators from Delaware and Maryland.

Three Black women — two Democrats and a Republican — have been nominated to run for governor in Georgia , Minnesota and the Virgin Islands . No Black woman has ever served as a governor in U.S. history. Another 26 Black women have been nominated to run for other statewide offices from 16 states.

As the motto for the United Negro College Fund states: “A mind is a terrible thing to waste.” Yet centuries of slavery and continuing discrimination after emancipation prevented most Black people from gaining the education, training and opportunities they deserved to fully utilize their brainpower.

Teaching enslaved people to read and write was a crime in most Southern states, although some still managed to become literate. After slavery ended, many Black children were forced to leave school at a young age to join the workforce to help their families farm or to take low-wage jobs, which were the only jobs open to them.

In the South, school segregation was mandated as late as the early 1970s — despite a 1954 Supreme Court ruling that it was unconstitutional. Black children — including me in Louisiana — were educated in dilapidated buildings with outdated hand-me-down books discarded by better-funded white public schools.

Black girls and women have had to battle sexism as well as racism. No women of any race could vote in federal elections until the 19th Amendment to the Constitution was ratified in 1920. And millions of Black women and men in the South — including my own parents and many relatives — were barred from voting until enactment of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 .

Rep. Shirley Chisholm (D-N.Y.), the first Black woman elected to the U.S. House in 1968, battled racist and sexist views when she ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. Few took her candidacy seriously.

“I have certainly met much more discrimination in terms of being a woman than being Black in the field of politics,” she said.

When Sen. Carol Moseley Braun (D-Ill.), the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992, briefly ran for the 2004 Democratic presidential nomination, she said it was “time to take the men-only sign off the White House door.” Four years later, a male senator from Illinois named Barack Obama became our first (and, so far, only) Black president.

I’ve never run for public office, but I have held plenty of governmental positions at all levels. Like generations of Black women before me, I’ve spent my life being told what I could not be, where I could not go, what I should not say and how I should not look and speak. And like many Black women, I have ignored those negative messages.

Black women are rising despite all the stereotypes and insults we’re still hit with — like the claim that we only advance because of diversity, equity and inclusion policies. We just keep moving forward, raising families, building careers, strengthening communities and our nation, and showing we can be leaders as well as followers.

Just last week, right-wing provocateur Laura Loomer proved that point, attacking Florida Senate nominee Angie Nixon (D), Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and several Black women in Congress — dismissing each as unqualified. It is the same insult dressed up in yesterday’s suit: If a Black woman succeeds, her success cannot be earned. We have heard it before, and we will keep answering it the same way — by leading anyway.

Black women have not suddenly become more capable. Our abilities are just finally being recognized. If more are elected in the midterms, they will help fulfill the hopes of the framers of the Constitution to “form a more perfect Union … and secure the Blessing of Liberty to ourselves and our Posterity.”

Donna Brazile is a political strategist, a contributor to ABC News and former chair of the Democratic National Committee. She is the author of “ Hacks: Inside the Break-ins and Breakdowns That Put Donald Trump in the White House .”

articles.title: Hillary Clinton ‘heartsick’ as Steinem, ‘architect’ of women’s equality, dies
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Thursday said she was “heartsick” over the death of Gloria Steinem, a well-known activist, feminist and “architect” of women’s equality. Steinem died in her New York City home on Wednesday. She was 92. “Oh, Gayle, I’m heartsick, as I think everyone who not only knew her but followed…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Thursday said she was “heartsick” over the death of Gloria Steinem, a well-known activist, feminist and “architect” of women’s equality.

Steinem died in her New York City home on Wednesday. She was 92.

“Oh, Gayle, I’m heartsick, as I think everyone who not only knew her but followed her, was inspired and challenged by her,” Clinton said in a phone call to “CBS Mornings” with co-host Gayle King.

She described Steinem’s activism as “rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice.”

“She was one of the architects of the entire structure of women equality,” the former first lady said. “I mean, tearing down those obstacles to young women being able to participate where their talents and hard work took them.”

Clinton credited Steinem for creating opportunities for many women over the decades, including making “it possible for Sally Ride to be an astronaut … she stood behind women in Congress who passed Title IX to open up opportunities in sports and academics for girls.”

“And she wasn’t on the Supreme Court when Roe v. Wade was decided, but her voice and her activism was behind that, and with all the setbacks that we’ve seen over the last decade or so, I want her voice to remain in our heads,” she added.

The former secretary of State also recalled Steinem’s support for Wilma Mankiller, the first woman elected principal chief of the Cherokee Nation. Clinton said she got to know them both and that Steinem would talk about how “what women have done for literally millennia to come together to work together, to help make life better.”

“She had this concept of signal fires, where people would signal by setting a fire on one mountain to the other mountain that something was going to happen or we need to get together,” she continued. “I’m trying to think of Gloria as an eternal signal fire. I really do.”

Steinem started her career as a journalist in 1963, covering Playboy under Hugh Hefner and profiling The Beatles’s John Lennon. Later that decade, she met women who spoke out in support of abortion rights. She told The Associated Press in 2022, after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, that this was “the beginning of activism for me.”

“Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy,” she told the AP.

She founded Ms. Magazine in 1972, which grew its subscriber base in the years that followed and continues to this day, published by the Feminist Majority Foundation.

Steinem faced backlash, once hearing a woman who called in to Larry King’s talk show on CNN in 1990 tell her to “rot in hell” for ruining “the beautiful American family.” Former President Nixon was once taped in the Oval Office ridiculing her magazine, prompting Steinem to call him “the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon” during a National Press Club event in 1972.

Criticisms from the president turned to praise decades later when former President Obama awarded Steinem the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

“Because of her work across America and around the world, more women are afforded the respect and opportunities that they deserve but she also changed how women thought about themselves,” Obama said at the time.

articles.title: Trump’s campaign funding colossus is the midterms’ biggest unknown
articles.summary: The Republicans’ cash advantage is staggering.
articles.body:
The midterms’ biggest unknown is when Trump will unleash his $400 million hoard. It is the biggest campaign war chest; it is also November’s biggest mystery variable. As Trump’s last important political campaign approaches, it has the power to significantly influence the outcome of his last two years in office.

California Democrat Jesse “Big Daddy” Unruh famously said : “Money is the mother’s milk of politics.” No one doubted that then; no one doubts this now. Seconding the sentiment while slightly softening the metaphor, ahead of November’s midterms, President Trump has a dairy farm’s worth at his disposal.

The Republicans’ cash advantage is staggering. Politico recently reported that Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., has over $403 million cash on hand. Trump himself recently claimed that he has raised over $850 million. And as huge as these sums are, they are only part of Republicans’ advantage. The Republican National Committee reported $128.5 million in cash on hand. In comparison, the Democratic National Committee reported just $16.3 million with $18.5 million in debt.

While these amounts change regularly, the scope of Republicans’ advantage is clear. Republicans’ three major fundraising arms and two affiliated super PACs have a reported $657 million in cash; Democrats have only half that at $334 million .

With the midterms just over two months away, the question is: When will this potential spending tsunami flow? That Trump has every incentive to unleash it is clear. Democrats put his administration through the wringer after taking the House in 2018. What’s more, during the last two years of Trump’s first term, Democrats didn’t hold the Senate. This time they could.

Democratic control of either body would eliminate Trump’s legislative ability in his last two years in office. Losing the Senate would end confirmation for his nominees. Losing the Senate and House would put him on the defensive across-the-board domestically. The stakes are huge and no one should understand them better than Trump.

While money favors Republicans, history does not, because the party holding the White House is overwhelmingly likely to lose seats in any midterm.

My calculations show that from 1926 through 2022, the party holding the presidency has lost on average 11.3 percent of its House seats and 6.7 percent of its Senate seats. Second midterms are even worse. From 1926 through 2022, I found the presidential party lost on average 12.9 percent of its House and 11.6 percent of its Senate seats.

Republicans have done all they can to mute the historical midterm impact. Mid-decade redistricting has netted them potentially 10 House seats . But these are just that — potential. There is nothing Republicans can do in this regard to protect statewide Senate races.

Democrats have helped Republicans somewhat when it comes to the Senate by nominating ultra progressives into some tight races in Michigan , Texas and Minnesota while seemingly botching others entirely in Maine (at least, initially) and Florida .

Conversely, with defeats in some primary contests, it is unclear how much Trump himself can help in some of these close races. What undoubtedly could help and remains to be done is for Republicans — particularly, the president — to tap their huge spending advantages.

Further bolstering the Republicans’ spending potential is the limited number of realistic targets. Republicans are guaranteed to win many seats; they are guaranteed to lose many.

The money available only needs to go to the comparatively small number of truly and potentially competitive seats. According to Cook Political Report , that means focusing on just 38 House seats. Even including the “likely” races adds only another 31 seats.

The Senate total is even smaller. According to Cook , there are just six tossup seats and six “likely” or “lean” seats.

An enormous cash dump beginning after Labor Day could greatly influence close races and prevent others from becoming close. Senate races in Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Kansas, Maine and Texas spring readily to mind. It would also allow Republicans to expand the field, and thereby, hedge their bets in places like Georgia and Minnesota.

Holding either house would be a major win. Holding both would be even bigger, and increasing majorities in both would be nothing short of a coup.

Nothing would smooth Trump’s last two years in office more than holding the House or Senate. Nor would anything likely have a greater impact on defining Trump’s legacy. This would potentially extend Trump’s influence beyond his time in office, leaving Republicans with majorities as Trump leaves the White House and a launching pad for even larger majorities beyond 2028.

It would also unscored his power in fundraising and what he can accomplish with it. This is not something to be taken lightly because it is a power that Trump can take with him when he leaves office. His ability to raise and direct resources could easily influence the 2028 primary and general elections.

Trump has every incentive to unleash the financial fury ahead of this November. He has all the means to do so. The question is, will Trump do so — and if so, when?

J.T. Young is the author of the recent book, “Unprecedented Assault: How Big Government Unleashed America’s Socialist Left” from RealClear Publishing. Follow him on Substack .

articles.title: Maduro claims immunity, asks judge to dismiss drug-trafficking charges against him and his wife
articles.summary: Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores argue sovereign immunity shields them from narco-terrorism and drug trafficking charges in a federal motion to dismiss.
articles.body: Former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores asked a federal judge Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking charges against them, arguing, among other things, that the pair have sovereign immunity, according to court documents. "No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought. That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own," a memorandum Maduro's lawyers filed in support of their motion to dismiss read. "That immunity flows not from goodwill that can be withdrawn on a whim, but from the perfect equality and absolute independence of sovereigns. Thus, this Court lacks jurisdiction with respect to Mr. Maduro, who is recognized by the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as its head of state," the document continued. MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM In January 2026, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed a fourth superseding indictment against Maduro and Flores. The indictment charged Maduro with narco-terrorism conspiracy, and both Flores and Maduro with cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. The indictment alleged that for decades, Maduro used his position — first as a deputy in Venezuela's National Assembly and then as the country's president — to conspire with narco-terrorists from some of the world's largest cartels to import cocaine into the United States. Maduro's lawyers, however, claim that sovereign immunity prevents the U.S. from taking action against Maduro. "The official character of these acts — such as issuing diplomatic passports, deploying the military, and announcing Venezuelan foreign policy — is apparent from the face of the Indictment. Because these actions were undertaken in his official capacity on behalf of a foreign sovereign, he may not be required to respond in this Court to the Indictment’s characterizations of his motives and intent in taking these actions," the document reads. STATE DEPARTMENT ANNOUNCES 'TOTAL COMPLIANCE' FROM VENEZUELAN GOVERNMENT IN RELIEF EFFORTS AFTER MADURO ARREST The U.S. government officially declared Maduro to be an illegitimate president in 2019 after Maduro declared victory in the disputed 2018 presidential election. Maduro's lawyers also argue that the indictment violates his and Flores' due process, according to court documents. The document asserts that Maduro "vehemently denies that he had anything to do with drug trafficking or intended to benefit anyone engaged in terrorism." The motion to dismiss then argues that the charges against Maduro fail to establish that his alleged crimes took place in or were aimed at the United States, and therefore do not meet the standards of due process. ARMY SOLDIER INVOLVED IN MADURO CAPTURE ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY USING CLASSIFIED INTEL TO WIN $410K IN BETS "The narcoterrorism statute, which was enacted in 2006 in connection with the reauthorization of the USA PATRIOT ACT, was intended to target foreign conduct. Recognizing that its power to police the rest of the world is not unlimited, Congress included a jurisdictional element that authorizes the use of the statute to prosecute foreign conduct under only five enumerated scenarios in which the foreign conduct is connected to the United States. Ignoring those parameters set by Congress, the Indictment fails — even by tracking the statutory language — to allege any basis for jurisdiction over the solely foreign conduct it alleges," the motion to dismiss reads. The U.S. apprehended Maduro and Flores during a January military operation, titled Operation Absolute Resolve, in which U.S. forces captured the couple in Venezuela's capital of Caracas and extradited them back to the United States to be prosecuted in New York federal court. TRUMP PICKS JAMES MCDONALD TO LEAD POWERFUL SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK AFTER JAY CLAYTON'S DEPARTURE Maduro is set to appear in court in November to begin oral arguments in support of his motion to dismiss. articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick apologized Thursday for saying on television that no Americans had died in the war with Iran, saying he was thinking about Venezuela.

“I misspoke. 18 members of our ​military have died, and to those families ⁠my heart breaks and I am so ​very sorry for their loss. I was thinking ​about the Venezuelan military operation where no service members died,” Lutnick said in a post on the social platform X.

Lutnick made the comments on CNBC on Wednesday while attending the Group of 20 finance summit in North Carolina.

“The way the president is playing Iran — there haven’t been American deaths, it’s really just an economic choke-out,” he said when talking about bond markets.

President Trump defended his Commerce secretary on Truth Social before Lutnick’s post.

“Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed,” Trump wrote. “18 people were killed in Iran!”

The Commerce Department did not respond to request for comment from The Hill on Wednesday.

Eighteen service members have died since March while serving at U.S. bases in the Middle East. More than 750 others have been wounded.

Lutnick also pointed to the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on New York City in his post. He was the head of Cantor Fitzgerald at the time.

“As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches, I am deeply thankful for our military and the sacrifices the men and women who serve our great country make, so such an attack, where I lost my brother Gary (36), my best friend Doug (39) and 656 other close friends and colleagues in the attacks on the World Trade Center, never happens again,” he wrote. “Never!”

President Trump denied allegations Wednesday that he wore a wig, citing an incident in 2024 where he faced windy weather.

During a speech at the White House Rose Garden dinner , Trump recalled when he spoke at a campaign rally in 2024 for Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), where he faced “the worst weather I think I’ve ever experienced outside of maybe a hurricane we had in Florida one time.” “I went up to the speaker, and it was blowing so hard,” he said. “You know, for years, I had to suffer with people saying, ‘He wears a wig.'”

“I don’t wear a wig. But that night, they found out I did not wear a wig because if you did, it was not going to be on your head very long,” Trump continued.

He described how during the event, teleprompters even blew off the stage as he walked up to the podium.

The Associated Press in 2024 reported similar conditions, saying the event was on a “wind-whipped airfield” in Vandalia, Ohio.

Comedian Rosie O’Donnell, who has feuded with Trump for years, remarked in August that Trump’s hair was a wig.

“You’ve got to realize it’s time to hang up your wig and let Natalie tuck you in,” she said during her third night filling in for Jimmy Kimmel on ABC’s “Jimmy Kimmel Live!”

O’Donnell was referring to White House aide Natalie Harp.

O’Donnell also performed a song while hosting, with one line saying, “Your wig’s a mess.”

Trump has asserted since his first term that his hair is real, even saying at a campaign rally in 2015, “I don’t wear a toupee; it’s my hair, I swear.”

“This is getting crazy,” he said as he pulled on his hair.

The president then called a woman onto the stage to feel his hair who confirmed his earlier statements.

articles.title: Billionaire Leon Black challenges House subpoena for Epstein testimony
articles.summary: Private equity investor Leon Black filed a lawsuit Thursday to stave off subpoenas demanding he testify and hand over documents as part of a congressional investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black was slated to appear the same day for a deposition before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee to answer questions about his ties to…
articles.body:
Private equity investor Leon Black filed a lawsuit Thursday to stave off subpoenas demanding he testify and hand over documents as part of a congressional investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Black was slated to appear the same day for a deposition before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee to answer questions about his ties to Epstein. The investor denies knowledge of any of Epstein’s illegal activity .

His lawsuit argues the committee lacks legal authority to enforce the subpoenas and that they improperly seek private information.

“Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the complaint states.

The suit was filed in federal court in the nation’s capital. It has not yet been assigned to a judge.

The committee’s leadership teased consequences for Black.

Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), the committee’s chair, said Thursday’s deposition would move forward with an empty chair for the billionaire.

“It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people,” Comer said in a statement. “Our investigation is examining how the federal government for decades failed survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s crimes and how Mr. Epstein sought to curry favor with influential individuals to avoid scrutiny.”

“Mr. Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation as he was one of Mr. Epstein’s fee paying clients and has several nondisclosure agreements,” the Kentucky Republican said, adding that he would speak with members of the panel about “next steps.”

But the top Democrat on the committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (Calif.), said it should move forward with holding Black in contempt, a process that, if successful, would refer the Epstein associate to the Justice Department for criminal charges.

“By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two Congressional subpoenas. Black gave Jeffrey Epstein over $180 million over six years. He funded Epstein’s abuse and trafficking of women. Multiple women have also accused Black of sexual assault. His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable. We must hold him in contempt immediately,” Garcia said in a statement.

Lawmakers have sought to question Black, who co-founded Apollo Global Management, about payments he made to Epstein totaling millions over years. The investor says the payments were for tax and estate planning, among other services, and he had no knowledge of any abuse.

In June, Black voluntarily appeared for an interview with lawmakers but walked out during questioning. The subpoenas were issued the same day.

The billionaire says he has complied with multiple document requests from the committee, sometimes known as OGR, but argues others are overbroad.

“And they have left Mr. Black with a Hobson’s choice: to surrender private and confidential information that OGR has no lawful authority to demand or to maintain his well-founded objections and face actual or threatened contempt proceedings and federal court enforcement of an overbroad subpoena,” his lawsuit states.

articles.title: Recalls, warning issued for popular squishy kids’ toys over ‘serious injury’ risk
articles.summary: Federal authorities have warned that the beads within them could cause a child to choke or experience an intestinal obstruction.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Popular children’s squeeze toys have been recalled over concerns of serious injury hazards related to the beads within them, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission has announced. The agency is also warning consumers to immediately stop using another similar toy, despite no recall being issued.

Recalls have been issued for Squeezy Dumplings from GIHNJSI and Rainbow Mystery Squishy Buns from OKK Trading.

Both products, pictured below, contain water beads, which, if ingested, could expand within a child’s body, the CPSC explains. This can lead to choking and intestinal obstruction, “resulting in severe discomfort, vomiting, dehydration, and a risk of death to a child.”

The Squeezy Dumplings were sold on Amazon in May and June of this year, according to the recall notice. The round, squishy balls have cartoon faces and glitter-like particles. The package looks like a bamboo steamer, with a label reading “SQUEEZY DUMPLINGS” and “SQUEEZE ME.” About 8,000 Squeezy Dumplings have been recalled.

Roughly 7,200 Rainbow Mystery Squishy Bun Toys, which were available at third-party stores throughout the U.S. from May through August of this year, have been recalled. Like the Squeezy Dumplings, these toys have glitter and cartoon faces, and packaging that looks like a bamboo steamer. The labeling says “Rainbow MYSTERY” and “SUGAR EDITION.”

If you have any of the above toys, the CPSC advises writing “RECALLED” in permanent marker on the product and its container, throwing it away, and sending a photo of the disposed toy to GIHNJSI_recall@163.com , if it’s a Squeezy Dumpling, or recall@okktoys.com , if it’s a Squishy Bun. You can expect a full refund, according to the notice.

There have been no injuries reported in connection with these toys.

Meanwhile, the CPSC is advising consumers to immediately stop using Squishy Bun Toys from Ivyapingdianpu, as they violate mandatory safety standards for toys.

These also contain water beads, but the CPSC said the company has not agreed to a recall or offered a remedy to consumers despite receiving a Notice of Violation.

These dumpling-shaped toys contain glitter-like particles and water beads, and have a cartoon face. They come in a steamer-like container with labeling that reads “SQUISHY BUN” and “Rainbow MYSTERY.” You can see an example of these toys below:

The CPSC said roughly 100 of these toys, which were sold via Amazon in June and potentially by other sellers, are impacted.

The agency asks that if your child experiences any injuries related to these Squishy Buns, or if you notice any defects, you report it to the CPSC. These toys should also be disposed of immediately, officials said.

articles.title: 911 professionals aren’t considered first responders — Congress should change that
articles.summary: While their locations may be safe, their jobs are anything but.
articles.body:
In 2019, Tim Teneyck, an Ohio resident, answered a 911 call from someone ordering a pizza.

“This is the wrong number to call for pizza,” Teneyck responded.

“No, no, no,” the voice on the line said. “You’re not understanding.”

Within seconds, Teneyck understood completely. Under the ruse of ordering a large pie with pepperoni, the caller was actually reporting a domestic violence incident. By cracking the code, Teneyck got the information necessary to facilitate an immediate and safe response .

About 450 calls are placed to 911 every minute in our country. As a researcher who has traced the nearly 60-year history of America’s 911 system, I have learned firsthand that 911 professionals like Teneyck are the ultimate first responders, saving lives and protecting health every day. But under federal labor law, they are improperly regarded as administrative workers.

The Senate has approved legislation that would reclassify 911 professionals as “protective service personnel,” a critically important reflection of their roles in our emergency response system. Taking this step should be a priority for Congress before this session ends.

The term “first responders” typically conjures images of police officers or firefighters racing toward danger, not individuals quietly answering phone calls. But while their locations may be safe, their jobs are anything but.

Nearly half ( 48 percent ) of 911 professionals report taking calls involving kidnappings or hostages. Forty-two percent have dealt with nonaccidental deaths and 37 percent have been exposed to situations involving serious assaults. Three in 10 have fielded calls regarding a suicide . When mass shootings happen, dozens of 911 calls come in waves, exposing call takers to a seemingly unending cascade of unimaginable horrors.

As one 911 professional put it, they answer calls “where a mother or father is hysterical or their teenager has hung themselves or overdosed; the female you get on the line who is literally in the middle of being beaten or raped—all those screams and visualizations get trapped in our head.”

The physical and mental toll this takes can be extreme. Compared to an average person, 911 responders are 10 times as likely to endure anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, suicidal ideation and depression. They have double the risk of mental health conditions compared to law enforcement officers. Yet they do not always receive proper training or support to handle these types of situations, which is devastating in its own right. In a survey, 5 percent of 911 professionals said they held themselves accountable for a tragedy that they believe occurred as a result of how they had responded to a 911 call.

Yet there has been little national effort to look after 911 professionals. My research reveals gender discrimination to be a root cause of these gaps in care and understanding.

Women were originally hired for 911 roles because they were considered quieter and better listeners than men. But entrenched misogyny also meant providing women with lower pay and fewer benefits. That imbalance remains. In stark contrast to their police officer and firefighter brethren, women today account for nearly 80 percent of 911 professionals. Sadly, they still face an unforgiving system.

Rep. Norma Torres (D-Calif.) — the only 911 professional serving in Congress — has described how during her tenure at a 911 call center, it was considered a punishment for a police captain to be transferred to work alongside her. Employees at 911 centers have reported that they are frequently called lazy or dumb . Shockingly, police officers routinely ignore 911 professionals — even refusing to answer their radios — making the task of protecting public safety even harder.

The misclassification of 911 professionals is directly related to gender discrimination. The Bureau of Labor Statistics and White House Office of Management and Budget classify 911 professionals as administrative workers. This aligns them with clerical assistants and receptionists — roles also disproportionately served by women — rather than police officers and firefighters. As a result, the highest-paid 911 professional earns about as much as the lowest-paid police officer. That also means many 911 professionals lack access to robust mental health supports and disability benefits they desperately need.

Eighteen states have stepped up to classify 911 professionals as first responders. That includes states like Washington and Arizona , where 911 professionals now have a path to access pension systems originally designated for other first responders, allowing them to retire at younger ages with full benefits. These laws also help states hire and retain more experienced 911 professionals.

The federal government must now follow suit. The Enhancing First Response Act passed the Senate unanimously on Sept. 10, 2025. It was one day shy of the 24th anniversary of the worst terrorist attack in our nation’s history, which was so devastating for 911 professionals and all of our heroic first responders. It is past time for the House to do its part. A bill that provides such considerable value without costing the federal government a thing should cross the finish line as soon as possible.

A 911 professional is “the first person you may speak to on possibly one of the worst days of your life.” At a bare minimum, the people answering those calls deserve our respect — from their callers, their colleagues and their country.

Rebecca Neusteter is the executive director of the Health Lab at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy. Her book “ 911, What’s Your Emergency? The Promise and Peril of Crisis Response ,” publishes on Sept. 15.

images.caption: Dispatcher Donna Bocik responds to a 911 call at the Collier County Emergency Services Center, Friday, July 11, 2025, in Naples, Fla. (AP Photo/Marta Lavandier)

articles.title: House Republican ‘pretty sure’ Lake Ontario name change ‘a troll’
articles.summary: Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-N.Y.) said President Trump’s decision to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” is likely a “troll,” casting doubt on whether the new name will stick even as the federal government and major mapping services move to adopt it. “I’m pretty sure this is a troll,” Tenney, whose district covers…
articles.body:
Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-N.Y.) said President Trump’s decision to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” is likely a “troll,” casting doubt on whether the new name will stick even as the federal government and major mapping services move to adopt it.

“I’m pretty sure this is a troll,” Tenney, whose district covers much of New York’s Lake Ontario shoreline, told TMZ when asked whether businesses in her district should begin switching over to the new name.

Trump signed an executive order last week directing the Interior Department and U.S. Board on Geographic Names to rename the Great Lake, which is shared with Canada.

The move came amid a rapidly escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada after negotiations between the two longtime allies fell apart . Trump imposed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports and floated the name change shortly after the failed negotiations.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, in turn, announced retaliatory, “dollar-for-dollar” tariffs effective Sept. 8.

When asked what she would tell businesses in her 24th Congressional District that are trying to decide which name to use, the Republican said locals appear to be sticking with Lake Ontario for now.

“I think a lot of our counties are just staying right now on course because they don’t know if this is really a permanent thing or really just a part of a kind of hardball negotiations going on between the president and the prime minister in Canada,” Tenney said.

“I don’t know how permanent people think this is right now,” she added. “I mean, name changes come and go.”

Tenney suggested Trump’s executive order was likely made to provoke Canada rather than permanently rebrand the Great Lake.

“Trump, you know, likes to troll people and put out name changes,” she said. “We’ll see how long this lasts.”

On his first day back in office, Trump signed executive orders changing the name of several landmarks, including the controversial change from the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

Canada has since rejected the lake’s name change, which does not require Canada or other countries to stop using the name Lake Ontario.

The new name has nonetheless begun appearing in the U.S. Google Maps and Apple Maps services both switched to Lake America for its U.S. users after the name was updated in the federal geographic database.

articles.body:
Beverly Aikins said Wednesday that she would “probably punch” Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for past comments he made about her son, Vice President Vance.

In an interview on “ Tomi Lahren is Fearless ,” Fox News host Tomi Lahren showed Aikins a clip of El-Sayed stating, “Can you imagine, he’s got brown kids, at some point he’s going to have a really awkward conversation with his kids, like, you made your career hating people who are different.”

“I think that man’s an idiot,” Aikins said about the video. “Those are my babies. I love those babies. I would do anything for them. I love Usha as if she were my own daughter.”

“I don’t pay attention to people like that,” she added.

Vance’s relationship with his mother was described in his memoir, “Hillbilly Elegy,” which detailed his upbringing in rural Kentucky alongside Aikins’s struggle with addiction.

Aikins — who attended the 2024 inauguration of Vance and President Trump — celebrated her 10-year sobriety milestone in 2025 at the White House’s Roosevelt Room with her son’s family.

In the interview, Lahren mentioned another comment by El-Sayed, who wrote on the social platform X , “So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…”

Aikins said people who made comments like those must be “jealous” of the vice president’s family.

“It makes me mad, honestly,” she concluded. “But in the long run I’m not going to do anything about it. I mean, you know, I’d probably punch the guy if I’d ever seen him, and then that would get me in trouble.”

The feud between the two started when Vance labeled El-Sayed as “very, very evil” while at a campaign rally in Detroit on Monday.

“There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today,” Vance said.

El-Sayed responded in an CNN interview the same day, saying, “Well, let me tell you what’s evil. Evil is the idea of starting wars when there’s peace. Evil is the idea of stripping away people’s healthcare when they absolutely have no other option. What’s evil is to do that, so that you can pass a tax cut for billionaires.”

articles.title: 33 House Dems break with Jeffries as party fractures over Israel
articles.summary: The House passed a bill to cut federal funds to colleges participating in boycotts of Israel, but Democrats argue it violates free speech rights.
articles.body: The House of Representatives passed a bill aimed at blocking federal funds to colleges that boycott Israel, with the vast majority of Democrats voting against it. All but 33 left-wing lawmakers voted to block the measure, which would "prohibit an institution that participates in a non-expressive commercial boycott of Israel" from getting government funding. It would also force universities that do get federal funds to affirm their students "are not unreasonably obstructed" from studying abroad in Israel. The measure passed 237 to 169, with all but two Republicans voting in favor. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and his top deputies were among the 167 Democrats to vote "no" alongside Reps. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Warren Davidson, R-Ohio. It comes as antisemitism continues to be a growing threat in the U.S. amid Israel's war in Gaza. CHAOS ERUPTS AS HOUSE PASSES $1.15T DEFENSE BILL WITH ISRAEL PROVISION: 'STOP STOKING JEW HATRED' Democrats have argued the bill is an infringement on the First Amendment, while Republicans hold it up as a way to ensure Jewish students feel safe at U.S. colleges and universities. Republicans have seized on Democrats' divisions on the issue, which has coincided with a far-left insurgency plunging the party into civil war ahead of the midterms. HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL Far-left Democrats, like the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), have attacked members of their own party who they view as not sufficiently critical of Israel. It's translated into some antisemitic incidents, such as a gay Jewish Democrat running for Congress in California getting run out of a pro-transgender rights march over his support for Israel's sovereignty. Scott Wiener told CNN that people in the crowd made references to his "Israeli handlers" while berating him, a well-worn antisemitic trope. DEM RUNNING FOR PELOSI’S SEAT MOCKED AFTER ANTI-ISRAEL HECKLERS CHASE HIM FROM SF TRANS MARCH Those divisions were present on Thursday morning as well, with Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., co-leading the legislation that his own senior Democratic leadership opposed. Gottheimer said of the legislation in a statement, "The goal of the BDS movement is the destruction of the democratic State of Israel, America’s critical ally in the global fight against terror. BDS has no place on college campuses or anywhere in our country. At a time when our Jewish students are facing death threats, being physically assaulted, and blocked from going to class simply for who they are, we must do everything possible to ensure they can learn safely, speak freely, and get the education they deserve." But progressives, including Rep. Jerry Nadler, D-N.Y., who said he otherwise opposes the boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel, called it an attack on the Constitution. "The First Amendment right to free speech does not apply only to agreeable speech. No matter how much I may disagree with BDS, and find it strategically stupid and morally repugnant, I will always fight to protect Americans’ right to speech with which I disagree," Nadler said in a statement. Meanwhile, House Rules Committee Chairwoman Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., said BDS policies at colleges created hostile environments by "marginalizing Jewish students." She said it was the government's duty to protect the equal rights of those students, who she argued were living in a hostile environment at schools with anti-Israel policies. CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS "They are discriminating against people of the Jewish faith," Foxx said. "Now is not the time for talk. It is the time for action." Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., said during debate on the bill that it was Jewish students who were often leading BDS movements on college campuses. "A vote for this bill is a betrayal of those promising young students...because they want to save lives, no matter their faith or ethnicity."

articles.body: El pasado 18 de enero de 2026, un tren Iryo que iba de Málaga hacia Madrid descarriló y varios de sus últimos vagones invadieron la vía contigua por la que circulaba un Alvia procedente de la capital de España hacia Huelva, chocando contra estos dos coches descarrilados. Las hipótesis acerca de lo que pudo acarrear citada catástrofe no cesan y según apunta el diario ABC de Sevilla, un informe de Inspección Técnico Ocular del Instituto Armado afirma que todo sucedió por la rotura de una soldadura en la vía de alta velocidad de la línea Madrid-Sevilla, concretamente en el punto kilométrico 318+681 de la vía 1. Este informe detalla que el carril derecho se quebró por completo en la unión soldada de dos barras de acero con tres décadas de diferencia: un tramo antiguo de 1989 (con el sello ‘Ensidesa 89’) y uno moderno colocado recientemente con el sello ‘Ensidesa 230. La soldadura se quebró y la barra más suave se soltó de sus anclajes y giró de manera violenta hacia el exterior. Los agentes determinaron que el carril no se rompió de manera inmediata al paso del convoy, sino que ya acumulaba desgaste anterior. Según detallan, tras la rotura, las pestañas de las ruedas golpearon los tornillos de fijación y, en la traviesa número 100, la inercia arrancó un fragmento de vía de más de dos metros, causando el descarrilamiento de los dos vagones del Iryo y colisionando luego con el Alvia que iba en sentido contrario. Pues bien, el ministro de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible, Óscar Puente, citó la información del rotativo mencionado anteriormente y se pronunció de manera tajante al respecto: “Bulo. No hay ningún informe. Solo un acta de inspección ocular, 9 meses después, que no añade nada nuevo ni establece ninguna conclusión. Para eso están las periciales, que aún siguen sin practicarse. Y los carriles que siguen sin ir al laboratorio”. Los usuarios también respondieron al político con algunos comentarios como “Deberías estar en la cárcel”, “No tienes honor ni dignidad" o “Afronta tus responsabilidades”.

articles.title: Contempt of Congress yields mixed results
articles.summary: A recent controversy involving Anthony Fauci’s refusal to testify before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs highlighted the complexities of congressional contempt power and its application within the current political landscape.
articles.body:
Contempt of Congress is one of those ephemeral things that floats somewhere between the Constitution and the rules of the House and Senate but is not mentioned in any of those foundational documents. Yet, as an “implied power,” it is one of the most essential tools parliamentary bodies have to carry out their lawmaking and oversight responsibilities.

While Great Britain can boast it is the only parliamentary democracy without a written constitution, the contempt of Parliament power has long been recognized there. That power was carried forward in the American colonial legislatures and then in the U.S. Congress.

It wasn’t until 1857 the contempt power became enshrined in one of our laws . That law reads, quite simply that any person summoned by either house as a witness to give testimony or produce papers and who refuses to do so shall be guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000 and imprisonment of up to 12 months.

Prior to that statutory enactment, Congress held its own trials to punish those who refused to cooperate with congressional inquiries. Congress even provided a musty jail cell in the bowels of the Capitol to imprison recalcitrant witnesses until they cooperated.

The most recent and dramatic example of a contempt case unfolded on Aug. 6, when the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), was holding hearings on the COVID-19 pandemic. Anthony Fauci, former chief medical adviser to President Joe Biden and prior to that director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, refused to respond to more than 100 questions put to him, instead invoking his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

Consequently, the committee voted along strict party lines to find Fauci in contempt of Congress. Paul vowed to take the contempt case directly to then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche for prosecution rather than first put the matter to a vote before the full Senate where a 60 vote threshold would be needed to pass the resolution.

What made this incident more bizarre was that Fauci had already received a blanket pardon from President Biden for any possible federal offenses relating to Fauci’s federal role that occurred between January 2014 and Jan. 19, 2025. It was a preemptive pardon in that no charges had been lodged against him. Paul thought that was a sufficient shield to obviate the need for invoking the Fifth. Fauci, on the other hand, viewed the whole inquiry as a set-up — a “perjury trap,” as he put it.

Even though Paul sent a letter to the Justice Department the same day the committee voted on contempt, he did not immediately file a formal referral request to Vice President JD Vance, in his capacity as president of the Senate, to certify the contempt. That was not done until Aug. 25.

According to a Wall Street Journal report last week , this has put the Trump administration in a difficult position. Trump is reportedly reluctant to press the Justice Department to act, for fear the referral might be summarily dismissed.

Trump said that although Fauci “made a lot of mistakes,” during COVID, he stopped short of saying he should be prosecuted. Moreover, he said he respects the presidential pardon as “a powerful thing.”

If the Fauci contempt matter is referred to Justice, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia will have discretion over whether it should be prosecuted. The Trump’s seeming ambivalence on the issue has allowed the Department of Justice some wiggle-room in its decision.

In the 117th Congress, Trump aides Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro were indicted, tried, convicted and imprisoned for refusing to testify on the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on Congress. Two others found in contempt, Mark Meadows and Peter Scavino, were not indicted.

In the current 119th Congress, former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton initially refused to honor a subpoena for testimony on the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. When the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee threatened to cite them for contempt of Congress, they had a change of heart and agreed to appear voluntarily in closed session to answer questions under oath.

The contempt power is still considered a “club behind the door,” both to encourage and threaten subpoenaed witnesses to appear and present requested documents. The fact that it is being gamed more recently does not detract from its importance in enabling Congress to conduct oversight by getting the information it needs to do its job in a thorough and fair manner.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” (2000), and, “Changing Cultures in Congess: From Fair Play to Power Plays” (2018).

articles.title: House GOP cuts 2 weeks from its schedule
articles.summary: House Republican leaders announced Thursday that the final two weeks of their September session are canceled, cutting the legislative calendar short ahead of the November midterm elections. Lawmakers are expected to reconvene on Sept. 14 after next week’s Labor Day break and remain in session through Sept. 17. They will then be expected to leave…
articles.body:
House Republican leaders announced Thursday that the final two weeks of their September session are canceled, cutting the legislative calendar short ahead of the November midterm elections.

Lawmakers are expected to reconvene on Sept. 14 after next week’s Labor Day break and remain in session through Sept. 17. They will then be expected to leave Washington and remain out of session until mid-November.

The House had previously been scheduled to remain in session through the end of September, but now it will no longer be expected to during the weeks of Sept. 21 and Sept. 28, according to a notice from the House Republican whip’s office.

The schedule change comes after the House voted Tuesday to send a short-term extension of government funding until December to President Trump’s desk, avoiding a politically risky shutdown before the midterm elections.

According to the whip’s office, members could still be called back to Washington during those two weeks if the Senate adopts a party-line budget reconciliation package , for which they will be given 48 hours’ notice.

The schedule change will allow lawmakers to spend more time in their districts as they enter the final stretch of campaigning ahead of November and Republicans fight to maintain their narrow House majority.

articles.title: Musk picks his first GOP warriors as a 2026 money surge takes shape
articles.summary: America PAC spent over $800,000 in 12 days backing Republicans, with Ken Paxton's Texas Senate race receiving the largest share of Elon Musk's cash.
articles.body: Elon Musk’s super PAC made its first major publicly disclosed burst of midterm spending, dumping significant amounts of cash over a very short period of time into races Republicans virtually must win to retain control of Congress. Between Aug. 19 and Aug. 31, Musk’s America PAC reported just over $800,000 in expenditures supporting Republican candidates and opposing their Democratic rivals — an average of roughly $70,000 per day. By far the largest concentration of Musk’s spending was in the Texas Senate race, where America PAC spent nearly $248,000 supporting Paxton and opposing Talarico. Republicans are heading into the midterms with a massive cash advantage, but are struggling to secure advantageous positions in even traditionally Republican states such as Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Ohio, according to Fox News’ Power Rankings. Musk opening his pocketbook for the GOP, an eventuality that was once in doubt given his prior split with the president, could provide Republicans with a much-needed lifeline as November approaches. JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH' The bulk of the spending went toward "printing" expenses paid out to Storytellers Group, a political vendor that specializes in direct-mail work. Over his 12-day expenditure period, Musk spent $123,000 opposing Talarico’s candidacy and about $125,000 supporting Paxton, according to a campaign finance filing released Wednesday. RNC CHAIR SAYS TALARICO'S GOP CROSSOVER HOPES ARE A 'PIPE DREAM': 'NOBODY IS GOING TO FOLLOW HIM' The spending, while helpful to Republicans, gives Democrats a new angle of attack to use in the districts where Musk’s PAC is deploying resources. Musk has suffered from low favorability ratings among Americans, and his efforts with the Department of Government Efficiency, likewise, proved unpopular. Democrats running in the competitive races where Musk is spending can now credibly tie their opponents to the billionaire. Talarico, for instance, has made running against billionaire interests a focal point of his campaign, a plank that increases in relevance now that Musk has waded into his race. AFTER PLATNER IMPLOSION, MAINE DEMOCRATS RUSH TOWARD NEW SENATE NOMINEE DESPITE FRESH WARNING SIGNS Musk’s PAC also spent a considerable amount in Maine’s Senate race, deploying roughly $135,000 against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson and about $35,000 to assist incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins. Collins has worked to distance herself from the Trump administration and national Republicans as she seeks re-election in a left-leaning state, an effort Musk’s spending could complicate. Other races Musk’s PAC spent in include the Senate races in Michigan, Ohio and New Hampshire as well as a handful of competitive House races in states like New York, Florida and Wisconsin. articles.title: Judge blocks new effort to limit birthright citizenship by Trump
articles.summary: A judge cited the earlier Supreme Court ruling blocking Trump's effort as precedent for blocking it again.
articles.body:
A judge has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship in the US, after the Supreme Court rejected his previous effort.

Trump signed a more narrow executive order after the high court's ruling, seeking to deny citizenship to children of "alien enemies" and those engaged in "birth tourism".

But Judge Deborah Boardman said this, too, was likely an infringement upon the constitutional right of automatic citizenship conferred to those born in the US.

Boardman issued a preliminary injunction on Wednesday temporarily blocking Trump's order, until a lawsuit brought by immigrant advocacy groups is settled. The administration is likely to appeal.

"The 2026 Executive Order is almost certainly unconstitutional," Boardman said, citing the Supreme Court's ruling on Trump's earlier birthright citizenship effort.

"This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President's most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them."

The lawsuit was brought by a group of immigrant rights groups, including CASA and Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project. They had sued over Trump's previous executive order that sought to end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants.

After the Supreme Court's ruling in June, Trump signed a new, more narrow executive order in August. The order targeted "birth tourism", the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies automatically are citizens.

It is already illegal to travel to the US for the purpose of giving birth, but the latest executive order aimed to enhance regulations and expand enforcement against the practice.

It also aimed to eliminate citizenship for children whose parents are considered "alien enemies", a term the administration defines as those belonging to designated terrorist organisations, including drug cartels.

Under the August executive order, children whose parents work for foreign governments in the US also would have had their citizenship denied.

Government lawyers argued that the Supreme Court's ruling in June upholding birthright citizenship did not preclude other, more narrow options to limit the right.

Exceptions have been allowed in the past, they noted, including for the children of diplomats and alien enemies.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Biden attempting to thwart President Trump's commonsense agenda," a White House spokesperson said on Thursday, according to BBC media partner, CBS News.

"The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

Trump's repeated attempts to eliminate or reduce birthright citizenship are part of a larger strategy to reduce immigration and migration to the US, which has included ending Temporary Protected Status for several countries and increasing deportations.

In August, US immigration officials made nearly 51,000 arrests, a new monthly record.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s super PAC dives into the midterms to bolster Republicans in battleground races
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s super PAC has funneled about $800,000 into battleground races across the country to boost Republican candidates.
articles.body: Elon Musk’s super PAC has funneled about $800,000 into battleground races across the country to boost Republican candidates. Musk’s America PAC is weighing in on highly competitive races, including the Senate contests in Maine, Michigan and Texas, according to a report it filed with the Federal Election Commission on Wednesday night. America PAC disclosed nearly a quarter-million dollars in recent spending on the Texas Senate race, more than $170,000 on the Maine Senate race and more than $25,000 on the Michigan Senate race. NBC News last week reported that the super PAC had started to spend on digital ads in Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire to support conservatives and compel people to register to vote. The new filing indicates that the billionaire is prepared to unleash more money as Democrats and Republicans barrel toward midterm elections, which are just about two months away. Democrats are seeking to flip several competitive seats in hopes of retaking one or both chambers of Congress. And the spending in Texas’ Senate race, although small when compared to the tens of millions expected to rain down in the contest between Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, comes as Republicans have raised concerns about the their nominee’s fundraising gap and called on outside groups to help fill it. Musk’s super PAC is spending money across the country in House and Senate races in more than a dozen states: Alaska, Florida, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC, said in a statement over the summer that it was “excited to again be part of the team” to support Republicans’ midterm efforts. “The president’s political team and the rest of the GOP apparatus have built a top-notch operation that will put Republicans in a strong position to buck history and retain control of Congress this fall, and we’re excited to again be part of the team,” he said in the prior statement. Musk was a major financial player in the 2024 presidential race, when he spent more than $250 million to support President Donald Trump and Republicans. The next year, he spent millions of dollars to boost a conservative Wisconsin Supreme Court candidate, who lost the race. Trump and Musk had a close relationship in the first months of the president’s second term, when Musk headed the so-called Department of Government Efficiency. Musk made appearances at cabinet meetings, and he appeared to have the president’s ear. The two had a brief, but contentious, falling out. Musk briefly threatened to create a third political party — the “America Party” — amid his frustration with Trump, but has not followed through. The two men have since appeared to be on good terms. Earlier this year, Musk traveled with Trump to China for the president’s state visit.

articles.title: Trump administration threatens to cut Smithsonian support in latest claim of ideological bias
articles.summary: The Trump administration is threatening to withdraw support for the Smithsonian Institution, accusing its leadership of presenting a “radical ideology” that weakens “shared American identity” in the latest effort to pressure the institution to change its presentations and practices.
articles.body: The Trump administration is threatening to withdraw support for the Smithsonian Institution, accusing its leadership of presenting a “radical ideology” that weakens “shared American identity” in the latest effort to pressure the institution to change its presentations and practices. The Department of the Interior sent a letter to the Smithsonian last Friday, which the department posted online, laying out the administrations’ criticisms of the institution and requesting an in-person meeting with its board. In the letter, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and White House domestic policy assistant Vince Haley noted that the Smithsonian “enjoys support for executive departments and agencies” before threatening to sever those relationships. “Those executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership by, for example, loaning artifacts for exhibits, enabling procurement processes and making discretionary grants,” the letter said. The Smithsonian Institution declined to comment on the letter and on whether any meeting has taken place. The Trump administration has made multiple attempts to influence the Smithsonian, which traditionally has operated independently of the political party in power in Washington. The administration officials alleged in the letter that the museum violated anti-discrimination law and developed a “culture of ideological activism,” and requested a meeting with board members “in person at your earliest convenience to determine how best to address the findings outlined in this letter and identified in the aforementioned report,” a reference to a White House report from July. That report characterized Smithsonian leadership as promoting an ideological stance that moved the institution’s mission “toward an extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.” The report targeted the National Museum of American History in particular, arguing that it “confronts visitors with materials intended to undermine faith in American institutions and the longstanding shared ideals of the American people.” The report, released by the White House Domestic Policy Council, argued that the Smithsonian, “under its current leadership and current interpretive ideology, cannot be trusted to tell America’s story honestly and in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic.” Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch told staff in a July email obtained by NBC News that the report “is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History.” He added that the Smithsonian’s work “is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story.” Later that month, Trump said he was ordering “warning” signs to be placed in front of the Museum of American History to “inform” people about the July report and correct “inaccurate information presented in the Museum.”
